teach.title: An order has no -t on it

notice.ask: Which word in each sentence tells somebody to do something?

teach.say: When one person tells another to do something, the verb takes a shape of its own: **the imperative (the command form)**. It is not describing anybody, so it carries none of the endings that describe — no -t, no -nt. *Numerā!* is not 'he counts', it is 'count!', said to the person standing in front of you.

teach.title: One person, an -āre verb: the bare stem
teach.say: Take *vocāre* (to call), drop the -re, and what is left is the order to one person: *vocā!* Nothing is added at all. The ending is a long -ā, and the macron does work here: the whole order is that one vowel.

show.say: vocā — the order to one person ends in -ā

teach.title: More than one person: add -te
teach.say: Two boys, one order. The same stem takes -te on the end: *vocā* to one, *vocāte* to several. That -te is the only thing in the word that says how many people are being told.

show.say: vocāte — the order to more than one adds -te

check.ask: Order more than one person to call.

teach.title: Other verbs keep their own vowel
teach.say: Every verb does the same with the vowel it already owns: *tacē!* (tacēre), *audī!* (audīre). For several people the -te goes on behind that vowel: *tacēte*, *audīte*. There is nothing new to learn — only which vowel the verb has.

show.say: audī / audīte — the -īre verb keeps its ī

check.ask: Tacēte, puerī probī, et mē ___! (audīre, to more than one)

teach.title: Stems ending in a consonant slip in an e or an i
teach.say: *Sūmere*, *pōnere* and *discēdere* have no vowel of their own before the -re. To one person they end in a short -e: *sūme!*, *pōne!*, *discēde!* To several, an i comes in before the -te: *sūmite!*, *pōnite!*, *discēdite!* Three common verbs shorten further and you will meet them later: *dīc!*, *dūc!*, *fac!* with no -e at all.

show.say: sūme / sūmite — short -e for one, -ite for several

check.ask: Order one person, then several, to take something.

teach.title: Order or statement?
teach.say: The order and the statement sit one letter apart, so read the tail of the word. *Pōnit* has a -t: somebody is being described, he puts. *Pōne* has none: somebody is being told, put! The same holds for several — *veniunt* they come, *venīte* come!

check.ask: Is *venī* an order or a statement, and what tells you?

core.text: To give an order, Latin uses **the imperative (the command form)**, *modus imperātīvus*: *Tacē!* = Be quiet! *Venī!* = Come! For one person it is the verb's bare stem — *vocā*, *tacē*, *pōne*, *audī* — and for more than one the stem + *-te*: *vocāte*, *tacēte*, *pōnite*, *audīte*. The person ordered is often named beside it in the vocative (the calling form): *Tacē, serve!*

An English command is the plain verb with the subject *you* left out: *Come!* *Sit down!* Latin does the same with its own endings, and it also tells you whether one person or several is being ordered.
Singular: the stem (-ā, -ē, -e, -ī). Plural: add -te (-āte, -ēte, -ite, -īte). Three verbs shorten: *dīc!* (say), *dūc!* (lead), *fac!* (do).

In the 3rd conjugation order and statement differ by one letter: *pōne!* (put!) beside *pōnit* (he puts). In the others the vowel is the same and only the -t is missing: *vocā* / *vocat*. No -t and no -nt means nobody is being described; someone is being told.

more.text: The learner's notes treat the singular ending as a variable -(e) that drops after a vowel, which is why a-, e- and i-stem verbs show the bare stem (*flā!*, *vidē!*, *venī!*) while consonant stems keep it (*pōne!*, *frange!*); the plural -(i)te keeps its i only after a consonant (*pōnite*, but *flāte*, *vidēte*, *venīte*). Weak i-stems drop the i of the stem in the singular but keep it in the plural: *accipe!*, *accipite!*

Ørberg cap. IV: *dominus imperat, servus pāret* — imperātīvus -ā, -ē, -e, -ī against indicātīvus -at, -et, -it, -it. Irregular: *es!* / *este!* (be), *ī!* / *īte!* (go), *fer!* / *ferte!* (bring), and *dīc*, *dūc*, *fac*. Latin does not put *nōn* before a command; 'don't' is *nōlī* / *nōlīte* + infinitive (*Nōlī mē relinquere!*), and a polite or third-person command uses the subjunctive. A&G §448–450.
